claim: YouTube's self-published 2025 US Impact Report states YouTube has paid over $100 billion to creators, artists, and media companies combined over 2022-2025, but provides no recipient count or breakdown among individual creators versus artists versus media companies, making the figure impossible to convert into a per-creator average.
stance_target: Aggregate platform payout totals without a creator-count denominator, and without separating individual creators from media companies, cannot establish typical creator income
scope_conditions: YouTube first-party data, global, 2022-2025; report commissioned and published by Google/YouTube, the entity being measured (conflict of interest)
quoted_support: In the past four years alone, YouTube has paid over $100 billion to creators, artists, and media companies (2022-2025).
region: Global figure in a US-titled report; no Southeast Asia breakdown

claim: YouTube states 55% of ad and subscription revenue goes directly to creators, artists, and media companies through the YouTube Partner Program, but this is a revenue-share ratio, not a per-creator income figure, and again does not disaggregate creators from media companies.
stance_target: Revenue-share percentages describe platform-level splits, not individual creator earnings
scope_conditions: YouTube Partner Program, self-reported, sourced to 'Google/YouTube Support Website'
quoted_support: 55% of ad and subscription revenue goes directly to creators, artists, and media companies through the YouTube Partner Program.
time_period: Not dated precisely within document (report covers 2025)

claim: Oxford Economics modeling commissioned by Google estimates YouTube's US creative ecosystem contributed over $60 billion to US GDP and supported more than 540,000 full-time-equivalent (FTE) jobs in 2025, but the underlying input-output multipliers and methodology are not disclosed in this report.
stance_target: Macroeconomic multiplier-based 'jobs supported' and 'GDP contribution' figures are model outputs, not measured payroll or headcount, and should not be conflated with a creator population count
scope_conditions: Oxford Economics modeling, commissioned by Google, US only, 2025; methodology not shown in this report, only attributed
quoted_support: YouTube's creative ecosystem contributed over $60 billion to the United States's GDP in 2025... YouTube's creative ecosystem supported more than 540,000 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs in the United States in 2025.

claim: YouTube reports the number of channels earning six figures or more in revenue (USD) rose more than 7% year over year, but discloses no absolute count of such channels and no total creator population, making the growth-rate claim unverifiable and non-convertible to an income distribution.
stance_target: Percentage-growth claims without an absolute baseline count are unverifiable and cannot establish the share of creators earning six figures
scope_conditions: YouTube first-party data, global, 2025 vs prior year; no absolute number given
quoted_support: The number of YouTube channels making 6 figures or more in revenue (USD) is up more than 7% year over year.
numbers: +7% YoY growth in six-figure-earning channels (no base N given)

claim: A Public First 2025 survey found 77% of creators who say they have a media and entertainment career report that career started on YouTube, but no sample size is disclosed and the population is self-selected (creators who already identify as having a media/entertainment career).
stance_target: Self-selected creator survey results reporting career origin, not representative of all who attempt content creation
scope_conditions: Public First 2025 survey, commissioned via Google/YouTube; no N disclosed; population restricted to those who already self-identify as having a media/entertainment career, a survivorship-selected subgroup
quoted_support: 77% of creators who say they have a media and entertainment career started that career on YouTube.

claim: Two named creator case studies in the report (Binging with Babish with 10.5M subscribers/2.9B views, and Art for Kids Hub with 10.4M subscribers/3.8B views) are presented as illustrative success narratives, both survivorship-selected outliers used for promotional storytelling rather than statistical evidence of typical creator outcomes.
stance_target: Individual named success stories in platform-commissioned reports do not represent typical creator income or career trajectories
scope_conditions: Two named channels selected by YouTube/Google for the report; not a random or representative sample
quoted_support: Within four months, I was making more on YouTube than I was making at my full-time job. And that's the point when I decided to call it quits and try to pursue this as a full-time gig.
numbers: Art for Kids Hub: 10.4M subs, 3.8B views
